Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

issues.item: Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the trigger set is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile: darkness and especially tactile/unexpected touch are more characteristic of direct interpersonal assault than of a loved-one trauma, and there is no accompanying memory or appraisal content that links touch or darkness to this trauma.

The lock-checking threat item and parallel checking-locks strategy suggest a home-intrusion or direct personal danger formulation. In a loved-one trauma profile, this can occur, but here it is not supported by any appraisals or memory content about preventing another loss, danger to family, or responsibility. As selected, these items pull toward a different trauma narrative than the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Within the allowed nodes, the strongest coherence is around hyperarousal and intrusive memory, but the specific combination of tactile triggers plus lock-checking behavior is difficult to explain as one coherent formulation for a loved-one trauma without any linked negative appraisal content. This is more than merely unusual because the selected items imply different threat contexts.

The trigger/threat pattern is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of trauma to a loved one. Tactile unexpected-touch triggers plus broad startle to nearby movement are more typical of direct assault or personal threat trauma, not bereavement-focused trauma, unless there is additional context not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: Door/lock checking and hypervigilant startle responses imply an ongoing fear of intruders or immediate physical attack, but the rest of the profile centers on intrusive memory and loss-related trigger content rather than a coherent physical-danger narrative tied to the loved-one trauma.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, Threat is strongly linked to Triggers and Maladaptive Strategies, but the selected threat items reflect personal safety/intruder danger whereas the only clearly trauma-congruent trigger is loss-themed conversation. This creates a poor match between the active nodes: the threat content does not plausibly arise from the listed trauma-relevant triggers.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, tactile triggering by unexpected touch is not impossible, but paired with the rest of this profile it implies a direct personal-assault or physical-threat theme that is not supported by the memory items or the loss-focused trigger item. This makes the trigger set clinically incoherent around the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Repeated door/window lock checking suggests an ongoing home-intrusion or personal safety threat appraisal. In a profile centered on trauma to a loved one, with memory items focused on reliving and no appraisals linking the event to current intruder danger, this threat item does not fit the dominant loss-based formulation and appears mismatched with the other selected items.

issues.item: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeatedly checking locks/doors/windows is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and the indexed trauma type (trauma to a loved one). The other selected items center on grief/loss reminders, intrusive vivid replay, and generalized startle, but do not indicate a home-intrusion, assault, or safety-compulsion theme that would make lock-checking a coherent trauma-linked strategy. As selected, this item appears to target a threat-management pattern not otherwise represented in triggers, memory, or appraisals.

vignette:
David is a 48-year-old married shopowner who came to treatment after several years of living around a loss he still experiences as if it has not fully ended. He speaks about the event carefully at first, circling it, then with sudden flashes of detail that make it clear how sharply it remains with him. The trauma was the violent death of a loved one, and what stays with him is not a general sense of grief but a set of moments that return with disturbing clarity. He can describe the victim's face, the setting, and the sequence of what he learned and saw with a precision that feels to him less like remembering than being taken back into it. At times he says it is "like a film" that starts playing without his permission. When that happens, he does not feel as though he is thinking about something from years ago; it feels immediate, as if it is unfolding again in the present.

In the first weeks after the death, David found himself unable to tolerate ordinary conversations that touched on loss. If customers in his shop began talking about someone who had died, even in the abstract or in the familiar way people exchange condolences about a neighbor or relative, he felt his body tighten before he had fully registered why. Stories about people losing loved ones did not stay other people's stories for long. They pulled him toward the images he has tried so hard not to revisit. He began stepping away from the counter under the pretense of checking inventory or taking a phone call. He also learned to avoid places and occasions that were overtly organized around grief. Funerals, cemeteries, and memorial gatherings came to feel unbearable. He would tell his wife he simply could not do it, and over time there were services he did not attend and families he did not visit because he knew the atmosphere, the flowers, the condolences, even the sight of mourners, would bring everything up too forcefully.

What is striking is how specifically reminders of victims affect him. It is not only his own loved one he reacts to. News stories, photographs, even passing references to someone who was harmed can stop him cold. He feels pulled into the scene in a way that is hard to interrupt. What frightens him most is the suddenness of it: one second he is standing in his store, ringing up a customer or straightening a display, and the next he is caught in a vivid replay. He has come to dread that sense of helpless transport, so he has organized more and more of his life around not thinking about the event and not encountering anything that might stir grief. If a conversation starts going in that direction, he shuts it down or leaves. If his wife brings up the person they lost, he becomes distant, lights a cigarette, and moves outside. Smoking has become one of the few things he feels he can do in the moment, something concrete to occupy his hands and mouth when he is trying to push away what is coming up.

These habits have narrowed his life. As a shopowner, he cannot fully control what enters the store, and this has made his workday feel unpredictable. A customer's offhand story about a funeral, a sympathy card on display nearby, or a local conversation about a death in town can alter the rest of his day. He becomes tense, watchful, and emotionally flooded. He describes strong waves of fear, anger, guilt, and shame that can come over him quickly, sometimes all mixed together. Ordinary sounds in the shop can make him jump hard enough to embarrass him. The clatter of something dropped, a sudden knock, the quick scrape of a chair, or unexpected movement in his peripheral vision can make him react as though something dangerous is happening. He knows the reaction is bigger than the situation calls for, but in the moment his body does not seem to know that. He has started positioning himself where he can see people approach, and when someone moves suddenly near him he recoils before he can think.

His marriage has felt the strain of these patterns. His wife has wanted to remember, talk, and sometimes attend grief-related events that matter to their family and community; David has increasingly refused. From his perspective, he is not being cold. He is certain that if he lets himself go near these reminders, the memory will take over and he will lose his footing. Still, he sees the cost. He has become more cut off, more irritable, more absent even when he is physically present.

He finally sought help after a recent grief-related event he tried to avoid became impossible to ignore, and he found himself overtaken again by the same immediate, vivid replay. What brought him in was not only how painful the memory remains, but the realization that he has built his days around escaping it and still does not feel safe from it. He says he wants "some way to keep it in the past," and what he fears most is that the next reminder-someone's story in the shop, a funeral he cannot avoid, the sight of another victim on a screen-will pull him back just as completely.
